title: Rebase, and when not to use it
objective: By the end of this lesson you can rebase a branch to keep a readable history, and you can state clearly the one rule that decides whether rebasing is safe.

blocks.text: Merge joins two lines of work and records that they met. Rebase does something different: it takes your commits and replays them as if you had started from the current state of the other branch. The result is a straight line instead of a fork.

blocks.caption: The same work, two shapes
lines: merge:      a1 ── b2 ── e5 ── m6  ← main
rebase:     a1 ── b2 ── e5 ── c3' ── d4'   ← feature
# c3' and d4' are NEW commits with the same changes and different ids.

blocks.title: Rebase does not move commits — it recreates them
blocks.text: The originals are not edited; new commits are written with new identities and the old ones are left behind. That single fact explains everything about when rebasing is safe: recreating commits nobody else has is tidying, and recreating commits other people already have is forcing a split reality.

Rebase your own unshared work freely. Do not rebase anything other people have pulled. That is the whole rule, and it is why the common convention is: rebase your feature branch onto the shared branch to keep it current, then merge the feature branch in when it is done.

blocks.caption: The everyday use
lines: git rebase origin/main       # replay my commits on top of today's main
git rebase --abort           # or back out entirely, at any point

blocks.title: Conflicts during a rebase arrive one commit at a time
blocks.text: A merge presents every conflict at once. A rebase replays your commits in order, so you may resolve conflicts several times — once per commit that collides. That is more work, but each conflict is smaller and you can see which of your commits caused it.
Interactive rebase: tidying before you share

blocks.caption: Clean up the last few commits
lines: # an editor opens with one line per commit:
squash d4e5f6 fix typo          ← fold into the commit above
reword 7g8h9i Add validation     ← keep the change, edit the message
drop  j1k2l3 debug print         ← remove this commit entirely

blocks.text: This is how a branch of eleven commits — three of which say 'fix typo' — becomes three commits that each do one thing and explain themselves. Do it before opening a pull request, never after someone has started reviewing it.

rows: Bring your branch up to date before sharing
The steps you took are not information anyone needs
Integrate a finished branch into a shared one
Records that the branch existed and joined here
Anything already pushed and pulled by others
It splits reality for everyone who has it

blocks.title: If you must force-push, use --force-with-lease
blocks.text: After rebasing a branch you already pushed, the remote will reject a normal push. --force-with-lease refuses if someone else has added commits you have not seen, so you overwrite only what you expected to. Plain --force does not check, and that is how other people's work disappears.

blocks.title: Rebase and tidy in a sandbox
steps: In ~/git-lab: git switch main && echo base > base.txt && git add . && git commit -m "Add base"
Run: echo a > a.txt && git add . && git commit -m "Add a"
Run: echo 'typo' >> a.txt && git commit -am "fix typo"
Run: git switch main && echo more >> base.txt && git commit -am "Update base on main"
Run: git switch feature/tidy && git rebase main && git log --oneline --graph --all
Run: git rebase -i HEAD~2      (mark the second line as squash, save, then write one message)
blocks.expected: A branch that now sits on top of main as a straight line, then two commits collapsed into one with a message you wrote deliberately. Compare the graph before and after — same work, a history someone can actually read.

cheatsheet: Merge joins and records that two lines met; rebase replays your commits onto another base
Rebase creates NEW commits with new ids — the originals are left behind
Rebase your own unshared work freely; never rebase what others have pulled
Common convention: rebase the feature branch to stay current, merge it in when done
Rebase conflicts arrive one commit at a time; --continue proceeds, --abort backs out
git rebase -i HEAD~N — squash, reword, drop, reorder before sharing
Tidy before a review starts, not after
If a force push is unavoidable use --force-with-lease, never plain --force

checkpoint.prompt: What does rebase actually do to your commits?

choices.A: Moves the existing commits to a new position
choices.B: Creates new commits containing the same changes, with new identities, on top of the new base
choices.C: Merges them and deletes the branch
choices.D: Compresses them into one commit automatically

checkpoint.explanation: New commits with new ids. That is precisely why rebasing shared commits is a problem — everyone else still has the originals.

checkpoint.prompt: Which is the correct rule for when rebasing is safe?

choices.A: Rebase everything; merges make history messy
choices.B: Rebase only your own work that nobody else has pulled
choices.C: Rebase only on Fridays before a release
choices.D: Rebase only branches with fewer than five commits

checkpoint.explanation: Unshared history can be rewritten freely. Shared history cannot, because rewriting it gives everyone who has it a conflicting version of the same work.

checkpoint.prompt: You have eleven commits on a branch, four of which are 'fix typo'. What do you do before opening a pull request?

choices.B: git rebase -i to squash them into commits that each do one thing
choices.D: Delete the branch and start again

checkpoint.explanation: The steps you happened to take are not information a reviewer needs. Interactive rebase turns them into a history that explains the change — done before review begins, not during.

choices.B: It refuses the push if the remote gained commits you have not seen, so you cannot silently overwrite someone else's work
choices.C: It creates a backup branch automatically

checkpoint.explanation: Plain --force overwrites whatever is there. --force-with-lease checks that the remote is still where you last saw it before replacing it.
